catalog_quote: There are two types of stress possible within a Yankunytjatjara word, both fully predictable. The auditory correlates of stress are relatively higher pitch and greater loudness. In decreasing order of prominence: (1) Primary stress normally occurs on the initial vowel of a word, and on the initial vowel of reduplicated roots. Directional prefixes to verbs behave as separate phonological words in that both prefix and verb receive primary stress. (2) Secondary stress is found on the initial vowel of di- and polymoric suffixes. [p. 27] ... In terms of classical phonemics, stress is phonemic even though it is predictable in morphemic terms, because potentially there could be a minimal pair like kutjupa-tjara/kutjupatjara, where the first member consisted of a trimoric root plus a dimoric suffix with an initial secondary stress, and the second was an unanalysable stem. [fn. 8, p. 332]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the first vowel (syllable) of every phonological word, including each root of a reduplication and each part of a directional-prefix + verb combination; stress is fully predictable. Secondary stress is morphologically placed: on the first vowel of any suffix of two or more morae. Long vowels count as two morae for stress purposes (p. 22).
new_statements.secondary_stress: On the initial vowel of di- and polymoric (disyllabic or longer) suffixes; no alternating rhythmic secondary stress is stated for monomorphemic roots. Footnote 8 (p. 332) notes that because of this morphological placement, stress could in principle distinguish a root+dimoric-suffix string from an unanalysable stem (kutjupa-tjara vs kutjupatjara), so it is 'phonemic' in classical terms though predictable morphemically.
new_statements.exceptions: 'normally'; reduplicated roots each take primary stress; directional prefixes to verbs are separate phonological words with their own primary stress; a separately stressed negator wiya and the particle palu behave as separate words on stress criteria (pp. 213, 258 area of the thesis text). Weak (unstressed) vowels are elided in fluent speech (sec. 2.2.4).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (phonological word); secondary stress is defined over suffixes, so the domain is the morphologically complex word; sentence-level emphasis not treated here. Douglas 1958 (Warburton dialect) instead gives rhythmic secondary stress on the third syllable, and Tabain et al. 2014 found no secondary stress in Pitjantjatjara - the secondary-stress detail is dialect- and analysis-dependent, the initial primary stress is not.
new_statements.identity_note: Goddard 1983 describes the Yankunytjatjara dialect of the Western Desert language as spoken at Mimili and around the Everard Ranges / Indulkana (SA) in 1979-1982, i.e. yank1247 itself. Douglas 1958 (also saved) describes the Warburton Ranges dialect = Ngaanyatjarra (ngaa1240), and Tabain & Butcher 2014 / Tabain et al. 2014 describe Pitjantjatjara (pitj1243, already in the catalog); these are sister dialects and were used only for context.

sources.locator: Ch. 2, sec. 2.2.3 'Stress', p. 27 (PDF p. 46); footnote 8 to ch. 2, p. 332 (PDF p. 351)
sources.note: Sec. 2.2.3 'Stress', p. 27: two fully predictable stress types; primary stress on the initial vowel of a word (and of reduplicated roots; directional verb prefixes are separate phonological words with their own primary stress); secondary stress on the initial vowel of di- and polymoric suffixes; correlates = higher pitch and greater loudness. Footnote 8 (p. 332) adds that in classical-phonemic terms stress is nonetheless 'phonemic' because a root+suffix vs unanalysable stem could form a minimal pair. Long vowels count as two morae for the stress pattern (p. 22).

Goddard 1985 as primary stress on the first syllable (incl. first syllable of reduplicated stems), secondary stress on odd-numbered syllables and on the first syllable of disyllabic suffixes, final syllables unstressed; notes Tabain et al. 2014 cast doubt on secondary stress; argues feet are bimoraic; quotes Goddard 1985 p. 14 weak-vowel definition (identical to thesis p. 27 wording).

sources.note: First syllable of the Pitjantjatjara word marked by pitch raising and extra duration; no evidence for secondary stress elsewhere in the word, against traditional descriptions with alternating secondary stress. Sister dialect (pitj1243), not Yankunytjatjara; already the deciding source of our pitj1243 entry.
